newsitem.title: ITALY: European team meets in Rome on way to Albania.
newsitem.headline: European team meets in Rome on way to Albania.

text.p: A high-level European assessment team met in Rome on Monday on its way to Albania for talks with the new broad-based government on how to help end the Balkan country's anarchy, diplomatic sources said.
The 11-member team, led by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, was mandated to visit Albania by European Union foreign ministers meeting in the Netherlands on Sunday.

Divided over a response to the Albanian crisis, they ruled out military intervention in the chaos-hit Balkan state but said in a statement that they were "strongly committed to helping Albania restore civilian structures and law and order."
In Tirana, embattled President Sali Berisha said he would ask the delegation to send police, food and economic aid.
"We will request a major assistance to rebuild our institutions, also a very quick humanitarian assistance...and economic aid," Berisha told French Europe 1 radio.

The assessment team is due to stay in Albania until Wednesday and report back on the composition of a planned advisory mission of experts on civil reconstruction, police and military matters and humanitarian and financial assiatance.
"The primary task (of the mission) will be to help the Albanian authorities recover the levels of administrative control," one diplomatic source said.

The team was meeting at the Foreign Ministry in Rome and was then due to fly to the southern port of Brindisi to travel to Tirana by Italian military helicopter. Its arrival in the Albanian capital was expected in late afternoon.

The team, led by the Netherlands as holder of the EU presidency, includes representatives from Italy, Greece, the European Commission and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The sources said its members would meet new Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and ministers of his unity government, set up last week in a bid to stem the lawlessness that has spread across the impoverished country.
Part of the team was also expected to visit the main port of Durres, which with Tirana airport would be a vital bridgehead in any effort to send humanitarian aid to Albania.
It was not clear whether talks would also take place with Berisha, whose removal is a key demand of insurgents who have taken control in several southern towns.
The insurgents blame Berisha for the penury of Albanians in the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes in the country, Europe's poorest state.
"Our efforts should be strongly helped by Europe," Berisha said in his interview with Europe 1 radio.

Asked whether he would ask the team for foreign troops or police, Berisha said: "rather police to start with, because they will work with our police. It's urgent because elections have been fixed for June".

Berisha bowed to international pressure last week to create the new government, led by Fino of the main opposition Socialists. He repeated in the interview that he would resign if his Democratic Party lost the planned early election.
